client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed lately because my final exams are coming up next month and I just don't know how I'm going to get through them. Statistics has been a nightmare all semester — I failed the last two quizzes and I honestly feel like no matter how much I study, nothing sticks. I'm not sure talking about it is really going to change anything, but I figured I'd try.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now — the pressure of exams, the frustration of feeling like your efforts aren't paying off, and maybe even some doubt about whether reaching out will help. That last part actually takes courage, and I'm glad you're here. Can you tell me a little more about what "nothing sticks" feels like for you — is it more like the material feels confusing, or more like your mind just won't settle enough to hold onto it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: It's more like my mind just won't settle, I think. I'll read the same paragraph five times and by the end I can't even tell you what it was about — it's like the words just slide right off. And then I start panicking about the fact that I'm not retaining anything, which makes it even harder to focus, and it just becomes this whole spiral.
therapist: What you're describing is such a classic anxiety spiral — the worry about not focusing actually hijacks the focus itself, making the fear feel like proof. It makes a lot of sense that you're exhausted by it. I'm curious, when that spiral starts, do you notice it happening in the moment, or do you usually only recognize it after you've already been stuck in it for a while?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: Honestly, it's usually after the fact — like I'll suddenly realize I've been staring at the same paragraph for twenty minutes and my mind has been completely somewhere else the whole time. By the time I notice, I'm already frustrated with myself, which just makes it worse. It's like I only catch it once the damage is already done, you know?
therapist: That phrase — "once the damage is already done" — really stands out to me, because it tells me you're being pretty hard on yourself in those moments, treating a wandering mind like a personal failure rather than just... what anxiety does. The fact that you *do* eventually catch it is actually a skill worth building on, not evidence that you're broken. What do you think you usually say to yourself in that moment when you realize your mind has drifted?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, when I catch myself drifting, the first thing I think is something like "great, you did it again" or "why can't you just focus like a normal person." It's pretty harsh, I know, but it feels automatic, like my brain just goes straight to that place before I even have a chance to think otherwise. I guess I never really thought of catching it as a skill — it always just felt like arriving late to a mess I made.
therapist: Those automatic thoughts — "you did it again," "why can't you be normal" — are so critical, and yet they feel like just *facts* in the moment rather than thoughts your anxious brain is generating. I want to gently challenge that framing of "arriving late to a mess you made," because a mess implies you caused something to go wrong, when really your brain is just doing what overwhelmed brains do. What do you think it would feel like to catch the drift and respond with something even slightly more neutral — like "there it goes again" instead of a verdict about your worth?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets it intellectually, but in the moment it just doesn't feel like a thought — it feels like the truth staring me in the face. Like, if I try to say "there it goes again," won't I just know I'm trying to trick myself, and then feel even more ridiculous on top of everything else? I guess I'm skeptical that swapping out words is going to change how real and heavy it all feels when the anxiety is already spiraling.
therapist: Your skepticism makes complete sense, and I want to be clear — the goal isn't to trick yourself or paste a happier label over something that feels crushing, because you're right, that would feel hollow. What CBT is actually getting at is something subtler: not that the thought is *wrong*, but that it might be worth treating it as a *theory to examine* rather than a verdict to accept — which is different from just swapping words. Can you think of even one time when that "you did it again" voice turned out to be louder than the situation actually deserved?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I mean... yeah, maybe there was one time. A few months back I forgot to reply to a friend's message for like two days, and I spent the whole week convinced I'd ruined the friendship, that she'd think I was a terrible person. But then she just texted me like nothing happened, and I remember feeling almost confused by that, like my brain had built this whole catastrophe that just... didn't exist.
therapist: That example is really significant — your brain constructed an entire catastrophe, complete with all the emotional weight of a ruined friendship, and reality just quietly didn't cooperate with it. And yet I notice that even as you're describing this moment of insight, there's something almost tentative in how you're sharing it, like you're not quite ready to let it land as meaningful. What gets in the way of taking that example seriously as evidence that your mind sometimes turns up the alarm louder than the situation warrants?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I guess part of me is worried that if I accept that my mind was just overreacting, it feels like I'm dismissing how real the fear felt in the moment. Like, it wasn't nothing — I genuinely thought I had ruined things with her, and that pain was real even if the outcome wasn't as bad as I feared. And maybe I'm also a little scared that if I start trusting that my anxiety is usually wrong, I'll let my guard down and then something actually will go wrong and I won't see it coming.
therapist: What you just said is really important — you're not defending the anxiety, you're defending the *reality of your experience*, and those are two very different things, and both can be true at once. The fear was real, the pain was real, *and* the catastrophe didn't happen — holding all of that together isn't dismissing yourself, it's actually a more honest picture than either extreme. I'm also struck by this idea that your anxiety is like a security system you're afraid to turn down — can we explore that a little, because I'm curious what "letting your guard down" would actually look like to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I think "letting my guard down" would look like... not checking my phone every five minutes to see if my boss has emailed me something critical, or not rehearsing conversations in my head before they happen. But honestly, even just imagining that makes me feel exposed, like I'd be walking around without a jacket in the middle of winter. The anxiety feels protective, even when I know logically it's also exhausting me.
therapist: That image of walking around without a jacket in winter is such a vivid way to describe it — it captures how the anxiety doesn't just feel like a habit, it feels like *protection*, like something you'd be foolish to give up. And I notice there's a real energy in how you're describing this, like this part of the conversation is touching something that matters deeply to you. I want to sit with that metaphor a little — because a jacket protects you from the cold, but what would it mean to have a jacket you could *choose* to put on when you actually need it, rather than one you can never take off?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, that image actually kind of stops me for a second, because I've never thought about it that way — like maybe the anxiety isn't the jacket itself, but more like I've forgotten I'm even wearing one. But here's what scares me about the idea of choosing when to put it on: what if I misjudge the situation, what if I think it's safe and it's not, and then something bad happens because I let my guard down? That feels like the real fear underneath all of this — that the one time I stop being anxious, that's exactly when things will fall apart.
therapist: That fear — that your vigilance is the thing standing between you and everything falling apart — is such a heavy thing to carry, and it makes sense that it feels so hard to put down. What I notice is that underneath all the worry about exams and emails and friendships, there's this deeper belief that *you* are the one responsible for preventing bad things from happening, almost like the anxiety is a duty rather than just a feeling. I'm wondering — has anything actually bad ever happened *because* you were anxious, versus despite it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. Because when I actually try to think of a time where the anxiety itself caused something bad... I can't really come up with a clear example, but my brain immediately jumps to "well, that's because the worrying worked, that's why things didn't fall apart." It's like I can't even consider the possibility that things might have been okay anyway, because what if I'm wrong and I let my guard down?
therapist: What you just described is actually the anxiety's most clever trick — it takes credit for every good outcome, so it can never be proven wrong, and that makes it almost impossible to challenge. It's like a superstition that's completely self-sealing: the fact that things didn't fall apart *becomes* the evidence that the worrying was necessary. I'm curious — if a close friend told you they'd been exhausting themselves with worry for years and couldn't point to a single time it had actually prevented something bad, what would you say to them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
